header.scope: Won: online membership billing only. Studio front desks still process on Global Payments, and phase two has no date and depends on a partner integration.
header.incumbent: Global Payments, through the studio software
header.tag_why: The contract sat unsigned with the controller for two weeks until Tobi ran one month of Corelane's own failed renewals, and it was signed four days later. Front-desk integration is the runner-up because that gap is why only half the business moved.

evidence.excerpt: Churn. They report member churn to the board every quarter, it had ticked up two quarters running
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: somebody finally split it into people who cancelled and people whose card just failed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: members who never meant to leave
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I want to say a third of the churn? Don't quote me.
evidence.label: opinion

trigger.insight: The buyer's problem was a board-reported churn metric, not payments. Recovery only became the topic once someone split churn into cancellations and failed cards. The number that started the deal is in Maya's board deck, but the rep only has a hedged guess, so we can't yet say how big the problem was.
trigger.messaging: For subscription businesses, frame M10 (smart retries) as recovering board-reported churn: "members who never meant to leave." Lead with this instead of M7's revenue-growth framing or M1's global opener.

evidence.excerpt: She said it was her call.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: The paper had gone to Greg and it sat with him for two weeks. Nothing.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: His signature's on it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Maya chose us. Greg decided whether anybody got chosen.
evidence.label: opinion

decider.insight: Maya chose the vendor, but Greg, the controller, decided whether Corelane switched at all. The rep only identified Greg's role when pressed, even though Greg had been silent for two meetings and had asked about termination fees twice. Our process was built around the champion and nearly missed the economic buyer.
decider.messaging: Build a controller-facing track: the recoverable revenue from their own failed renewals, set against the cost of switching and exiting the incumbent. Get it in front of finance before the paper goes to them.

evidence.excerpt: What Maya told me is that they came back with a rate review and a new terminal bundle for the front desks, on a longer contract.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before that meeting it was all failed payments and retries.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: After it was, what readers do you have, do they work inside our studio software, what's the contract term, what does it cost to get out.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Greg asked about termination fees twice.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: According to Maya, the incumbent did not compete on recovery. It moved the fight to the front desk (terminals, studio-software fit) and to contract lock-in, which are where we are weakest. That worked: Global still holds the studios. "Rattled" is only the rep's read. We don't know whether Corelane accepted the longer terminal contract, and if they did, it may block phase two.
competitor.messaging: Prepare for incumbent counters with a staged-switch story: move online membership billing now with no front-desk or exit-fee exposure, and keep the conversation on recovery rather than letting it drift to hardware.

evidence.excerpt: Tobi, took an export of one month of their failed renewals and showed which ones were the kind that usually come back with a retry or an updated card.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Their file, not our average.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence. I opened with the global slide.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: is that the readers?
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: Our proof landed when it used their data. Our averages and our positioning did not. The global opener (M1) met silence at a US-plus-a-few-Canadian-studios business. "Unified commerce" (M3) was heard as hardware, and that invited the front-desk demand we couldn't meet. Pitching M3 effectively opened up our biggest gap.
message.messaging: For domestic subscription prospects, replace the M1 opener with a failed-renewal analysis on their own export. Retire "unified commerce" as a phrase, and describe the actual workflow only where we can demo it.

evidence.excerpt: Before that I honestly thought we were there to keep the incumbent honest.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Greg hadn't said a word in two meetings, and he asked for the spreadsheet.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Then we did the data session, and four days later it was signed.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The deal was stalled with finance, not lost on features. The thing that unstuck it was a spreadsheet Greg could take away and own. We don't know what was in it that convinced him, or whether limiting scope to online billing (which avoids front-desk exit fees) was the real enabler.
decided.messaging: Make the own-data recovery session a standard stage that finance owns, with a takeaway spreadsheet. Don't rely on M6's independent study or M4's average uplift for the money person.

evidence.excerpt: They asked to see our reader working inside their studio management software.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We couldn't show that live. It runs through a partner integration, and the partner did a call the week after.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: the studio managers will revolt
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: They saw the partner's demo. Not in their own setup.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: The rep says the gap "nearly cost us", but it actually did cost us the in-store half. The front desks stayed with Global, and phase two depends on a partner integration that has never been shown in Corelane's setup. A one-screen front desk ("check a member in, sell a water bottle") is a hard requirement, and M3 claims it without proof.
gaps.messaging: Until the partner integration can be demoed live inside common studio software, position as "online membership billing now, front desk via partner integration" rather than claiming one platform across tills and web.

evidence.excerpt: members who never meant to leave
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: is that the readers?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: the studio managers will revolt
evidence.label: quote

language.insight: The question was cut off and deferred to Slack (T30), so it was never answered. The quotes cited here surfaced in other answers.

gaps.question: What exact words did they use for their problem?
gaps.follow_up: Rep, over Slack as agreed: what words did Maya and Greg each use for failed-payment churn and for the front-desk requirement? Verbatim only.

gaps.question: How big was the failed-payment bucket?
gaps.follow_up: Rep: ask Maya for the failed-card share of churn from her board deck.

gaps.question: What in the spreadsheet convinced Greg, and did termination fees drive the online-only scope?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tobi what the analysis showed. Ask the rep, or Greg directly, whether avoiding Global's exit fees was why only memberships were signed.

gaps.question: Did Corelane accept Global's terminal bundle and longer contract?
gaps.follow_up: Rep: ask Maya what happened to Global's offer and when any front-desk contract term ends.

gaps.question: When is phase two, and what must the partner integration prove?
gaps.follow_up: Rep and partner manager: what is the acceptance test for the reader inside Corelane's studio software, and who owns the date?

close.rep_takeaway: Your best move was getting Tobi to run their own failed renewals. Make that the opener next time instead of the global slide. Also find the money person early: Greg was silent for two meetings and asked about termination fees twice, and that was the signal that he decided whether anyone switched. Finally, call a partial win partial. Global still has the front desks, so phase two is still an open deal.
